evidence: The authors state that changing configuration can be 'too disruptive' without proper domain knowledge, and their strategy focuses on incrementally adding training data to rebuild the model without changing the configuration.

actionable: Use the ElasTest platform for end-to-end testing of large complex cloud applications.
impact: Improved test coverage, detection of functional and non-functional behaviors at system level, and compatibility among all interacting components and involved infrastructures.
evidence: The ElasTest platform focuses on end-to-end testing of large complex cloud applications, which poses many challenges as it aims to expose functional and non-functional behaviors at system level to ensure compatibility among all interacting components and involved infrastructures (Section 2).
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Leverage the ElasTest platform for test automation throughout the test process cycle.
impact: Reduced manual effort, increased efficiency, and improved accuracy in testing activities.
evidence: The core of ElasTest is a solution for test automation all along the test process cycle, including SUT deployment, test execution, SUT monitoring during test run, and test results reporting to testers (Section 2).
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Utilize ElasTest for service mocking, environment virtualization, simulation, and test job parallelization.
impact: Comprehensive testing capabilities addressing various goals in a unified solution.
evidence: ElasTest ambitions to develop one solution that can cover all-in-one those four testing goals: service mocking (including database usage, IoT devices, and also user impersonation) and environment virtualization are already available. Simulation (concerning, e.g., network failures and stress load for scalability testing) and test job parallelization are under way at the time of writing (Section 2).
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Implement an approximate algorithm for detecting semantic clones by reducing the graph similarity problem to a tree similarity problem.
impact: Locates significantly more clones, which are often more semantically interesting than simple copied and pasted code fragments.
evidence: Compared with previous approaches, our tool locates significantly more clones in several million-line open source projects, including the Linux kernel.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Use semantic clone detection tools to identify redundant code fragments for refactoring and analyze them for consistent usage to locate bugs.
impact: Improves code maintainability by identifying redundancy and locating potential bugs.
evidence: Section 1 states that located clones can be used to 'identify redundant code to use as candidates for refactoring, and to be analyzed for consistent usage for the purpose of bug detection.'
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Configure clone detection tools with a minimum vector size of at least 8 statement nodes when analyzing large codebases.
impact: Eliminates false positives in clone detection results.
evidence: The authors found a false positive rate of 2 in 30 when the minimum was set to 4, but found no false positives in random samples when set to 8 or more (Section 5.2).
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Treat frequently occurring semantic clone patterns as implicit specifications to verify consistency across the codebase and identify deviations.
impact: Enables proactive bug finding by identifying violations of established data access patterns.
evidence: The authors observed specific data access patterns in PostgreSQL with high frequency and complexity, noting they are likely prescriptive and can be used as a specification for bug finding (Section 5.3).
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Augment existing fault localization and automatic program repair techniques with domain-specific information to handle complex algorithmic fixes.
impact: Enables effective detection and repair of bugs that typically require extensive, non-trivial code modifications.
evidence: Finding 1 reports that incorrect algorithm implementations cause 27.86% of AV bugs and involve an average of 104 lines of code, which are highly challenging for current state-of-the-art techniques.

actionable: Shift software testing and analysis focus from solely the Perception component to the Planning component.
impact: Targets the module with the highest bug density and the greatest concentration of safety-critical driving symptoms, improving overall system reliability.
evidence: Finding 13 identifies Planning as containing 27.05% of all bugs and 62.14% of driving-related symptoms, while current research heavily concentrates only on Perception's object detection sub-component.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Develop automated tools to manage upstream dependency updates and build configurations.
impact: Reduces the substantial maintenance burden caused by compilation failures and compatibility issues, freeing developer time for core functionality.
evidence: Findings 2 and 8 show that incorrect configurations cause 27.25% of bugs, with 58.09% of those instances resulting in build errors across both studied systems.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Adopt a governance style for pull request evaluation (protective, equitable, or lenient) that aligns with the community's culture and objectives.
impact: Effective PR governance ensures high-quality code changes are merged, contributing to software quality sustainability.
evidence: Survey findings from twelve FOSS communities revealed three distinct governance styles that safeguard software quality.
CATEGORY: Community Collaboration and Engagement | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Implement a continuous improvement process to develop and enhance quality assurance practices within the community.
impact: Continuous improvement demonstrates a community's ability to evolve and sustain software quality over time.
evidence: The ROS community successfully implemented a change method derived from participatory action research, showing that FOSS communities can collaborate on improving QA practices.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Community Collaboration and Engagement | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Encourage active participation strategies combining pecuniary and non-pecuniary contributions among community members.
impact: Active participation enhances community sustainability by reducing the strain caused by passive or latent participants.
evidence: The study observed that passive participation in ROS and Linux communities hinders growth and innovation, advocating for active strategies.

actionable: Adopt good PR evaluation practices (e.g., engagement with the PR and communication) to encourage participation and enhance contributors' retention.
impact: Improves contributors' retention, ensuring an adequate number of participants, which are the most valuable resource for FOSS software development.
evidence: Volunteers management literature suggests that adoption of good practices and enriching the volunteer experience determine retention, as reported in the article.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Community Collaboration and Engagement

actionable: Implement robust code review practices to foster high-quality contributions and collaboration within the community.
impact: Code reviews enhance software quality by leveraging contributors' passion and care for the project.
evidence: Research showed that intrinsic motivation and social attributes during code reviews drive excellence in FOSS projects.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Community Collaboration and Engagement

actionable: Trim effort outliers in software change data before applying effort-aware defect prediction models.
impact: Improves the alignment between classification capability and effort-aware performance, as shown by a moderate positive correlation (r=0.575) after trimming.
evidence: Experiments with six open-source datasets showed that trimming outliers improved the relationship between AUC and Popt metrics.

actionable: Use CSlicerCloud for identifying relevant commits implementing a specific functionality by providing test cases as slicing criteria.
impact: CSlicerCloud can identify the set of commits required for back-porting a functionality to earlier versions, ensuring correct execution and avoiding unnecessary changes.
evidence: The tool was evaluated on 10 open-source projects, achieving high precision and recall in identifying relevant commits (75/98 cases found all developer-annotated commits).

actionable: Apply semantic history slicing with feature test cases to locate specific commits for cherry-picking into release branches during new release cycles.
impact: Ensures that selected commits will pass tests and avoid merge conflicts when migrated to the release branch.
evidence: The text explicitly states that CSlicerCloud 'analyses the change history since the last release and uses feature test cases to locate the desired set of commits which guarantee not to cause merge conflicts and pass the tests when moved to the release branch.'
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Project Management and Governance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Use CSlicerCloud for creating logically clean and easy-to-merge pull requests by automatically computing the required changes and avoiding unnecessary changes.
impact: Improves efficiency, reduces errors in creating pull requests
evidence: Study found that CSlicerCloud can effectively avoid including unnecessary changes when ensuring correct execution of desired functionalities. (Section 1)
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Construct dependency networks for R CRAN.
impact: Increased developers' visibility over software, which helps evaluate risks for software.
evidence: Dependency networks have been constructed for R CRAN and shown to help evaluate risks for software.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Project Management and Governance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Measure the amount of knowledge transferred between developers using formula (1).
impact: Ability to weigh the flow of knowledge transfer between developers.
evidence: Formula (1) has been proposed and shown to measure the strength of expertise flow from one developer to another based on their contributions to files.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Community Collaboration and Engagement | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Set the direction of knowledge flow by determining who is the mentor and who is the follower.
impact: Ability to set the direction of the flow of knowledge transfer between developers.
evidence: A method has been proposed to determine the direction of the flow based on the first change to a file.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Community Collaboration and Engagement

actionable: Apply the ENCAPSULATE FIELD refactoring first if clients or subclasses access inherited fields.
impact: Removes the impediment of inaccessible inherited fields after removing inheritance, making the refactoring applicable.
evidence: Section 3.1.3 states that removing inheritance makes inherited fields vanish from the interface, and applying ENCAPSULATE FIELD first can remove this impediment.

actionable: Replace inheritance with delegation or composition to reduce interface bloat and strong coupling.
impact: Removes inappropriate subtyping, preserves encapsulation of the delegator and delegatee, allows dynamic replacement of the delegatee, and emulates multiple inheritance in single-inheritance languages.
evidence: The authors demonstrate that replacing Stack's inheritance from Vector with delegation solves contract violations and interface bloat, explicitly stating that delegation preserves encapsulation while inheritance breaks it (Section 2).

actionable: Prefer forwarding over true delegation when possible.
impact: Avoids hidden subclassing and preserves more flexibility for dynamic replacement of the delegatee.
evidence: Section 3.1.2 states that forwarding is preferred because it avoids secret subclassing, and Section 5.1 shows delegation is only necessary in 37% of applicable cases (or 15% without JHotDraw).

actionable: Generalize causing supertypes using the INFER TYPE refactoring to reduce imposed dead methods.
impact: Increases the gain of the refactoring by reducing the number of unneeded dead methods required by subtyping constraints.
evidence: Section 5.2 reports that subtyping constraints counteract the refactoring's purpose, and generalizing supertypes makes sense to increase the gain.

actionable: Use an inner subclass of the superclass and reverse delegation to achieve true delegation in Java, enabling open recursion.
impact: Increased applicability of the refactoring, allowing it to be used even when forwarding is not sufficient.
evidence: Figure 7 and accompanying text show how this technique works and its benefits.

article_title: **A Large-Scale Empirical Study on Vulnerability Distribution within Projects and the Lessons Learned**
actionable: Localize vulnerable code snippets and construct call graphs to explore semantic relations between vulnerabilities within a project.
impact: Enhances understanding of vulnerability distribution, dependency, and recurrence, facilitating more effective vulnerability detection and patching.
evidence: The study constructed VCGs (Vulnerability Call Graphs) for each project to represent semantic relations between vulnerable functions.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

article_title: **A Large-Scale Empirical Study on Vulnerability Distribution within Projects and the Lessons Learned**
actionable: Prioritize code review targets on functions that exhibit dependency relations (e.g., common parent, common child, or one-jump call) with known vulnerable functions.
impact: Facilitates the discovery of new zero-day vulnerabilities by leveraging spatial locality and semantic correlations.
evidence: Applying this strategy in ImageMagick led to the discovery of CVE-2019-7175 and four other new vulnerabilities; Finding 8 confirms >60% of vulnerable functions have a call-relation to another vulnerable function within a distance of 2.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

article_title: **A Large-Scale Empirical Study on Vulnerability Distribution within Projects and the Lessons Learned**
actionable: Enhance dynamic fuzzing tools by directing seed selection and assigning higher mutation priorities to functions located within high-density vulnerability clusters (k-clusters).
impact: Increases the efficiency and success rate of automated vulnerability discovery.
evidence: Integrating this approach into AFL for FFmpeg resulted in five new vulnerabilities; Finding 8 demonstrates that >80% of vulnerable functions in each project assemble within a single 2-cluster.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

article_title: **A Large-Scale Empirical Study on Vulnerability Distribution within Projects and the Lessons Learned**
actionable: Prioritize security audits and code reviews on the top vulnerability types historically prevalent in a project.
impact: Enables efficient allocation of security analysis resources to the most frequent risk categories based on stable historical patterns.
evidence: Finding 4 shows 70% of vulnerabilities fall into 20% of types, and Finding 5 confirms these top types remain stable over time; the authors explicitly suggest analysts can spend prioritized efforts auditing these popular types.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

article_title: **A Large-Scale Empirical Study on Vulnerability Distribution within Projects and the Lessons Learned**
actionable: Strengthen patch review processes to rigorously verify that fixes are complete and do not introduce new security risks.
impact: Prevents the recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same function caused by incomplete or flawed patches.
evidence: Finding 11 identifies incomplete fixes/fix introduction as a primary cause of vulnerability recurrence, with high-frequency vulnerable functions averaging 3 recurrences over ~515 days; the authors explicitly raise an alarm for developers to pay more attention to patch security.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Project Management and Governance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Use SARD to pre-select tuning parameters based on their influence on performance.
impact: Reduces the search space and improves autotuning efficiency.
evidence: SARD was used to pre-select tuning parameters for PostgreSQL, focusing on those affecting query execution.

actionable: Expose program's tuning parameters and sections to the autotuner using AtuneRT's API.
impact: Enables on-line autotuning for performance optimization.
evidence: AtuneRT's API is used for exposing PostgreSQL's tuning parameters and reconfiguring the program at run-time.

actionable: Constrain parameter search spaces by defining reasonable minimum and maximum value limits during configuration.
impact: Eliminates unreasonable search regions and prevents the autotuner from wasting time on ineffective configurations.
evidence: The authors limited parameters like work_mem (1 MB to 128 MB) and effective_io_concurrency (1 to 4), which helped manage the search space effectively as shown in Table 1.

actionable: Use the Nelder-Mead simplex algorithm for autotuning in discrete search spaces.
impact: Improved performance through smart probing of tuning parameter intervals.
evidence: Nelder-Mead simplex algorithm was modified to work on a discrete search space and used to find good enough parameter values for PostgreSQL's tuning parameters.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

article_title: **Poster: Git Blame Who?: Stylistic Authorship Attribution of Small, Incomplete Source Code Fragments**
actionable: Avoid open source contributions if attribution poses a risk.
impact: Reduces the risk of authorship attribution.
evidence: The article explicitly recommends this to mitigate risks, supported by their findings on accurate attribution even with small fragments.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

article_title: **Poster: Git Blame Who?: Stylistic Authorship Attribution of Small, Incomplete Source Code Fragments**
actionable: Use single line patches instead of blocks of code for open source contributions.
impact: Reduced likelihood of successful code authorship attribution, making it harder to trace contributions back to the contributor.
evidence: The study suggested that using single line patches instead of blocks of code can help minimize the risk of successful code authorship attribution.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Code Standards and Maintainability | Community Collaboration and Engagement

article_title: **Poster: Git Blame Who?: Stylistic Authorship Attribution of Small, Incomplete Source Code Fragments**
actionable: Do not rely on a single pseudonymous account to mask your identity across multiple contributions; avoid linking stylistic samples to one account.
impact: Prevents the aggregation of code fragments that enables high-confidence authorship attribution and preserves pseudonymity.
evidence: The text warns that 'a single pseudonymous account is not sufficient' because accumulating contributions allows samples to be linked, driving attribution accuracy up to 95% for pairs and 99% for sets of 15.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

article_title: **Poster: Git Blame Who?: Stylistic Authorship Attribution of Small, Incomplete Source Code Fragments**
actionable: Use a random forest classifier with 500 trees for source code authorship attribution.
impact: Increased accuracy in attributing source code samples, as shown in the article's experiments.
evidence: The study found that using a random forest classifier with 500 trees resulted in 73% overall accuracy for single samples and up to 99% accuracy for sets of 15 samples.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

article_title: **Poster: Git Blame Who?: Stylistic Authorship Attribution of Small, Incomplete Source Code Fragments**
actionable: Average output probability distributions across linked samples when performing attribution.
impact: Improved attribution accuracy, as demonstrated in the article's experiments.
evidence: The study showed that aggregating classifications for linked samples resulted in 70% accuracy for single samples, 95% accuracy for pairs of samples, and 99% accuracy for sets of 15 samples.

article_title: **Poster: Git Blame Who?: Stylistic Authorship Attribution of Small, Incomplete Source Code Fragments**
actionable: Use calibration curves to perform attribution in open world cases and with lower overall accuracy.
impact: Enhanced ability to identify the author of even small, single code contributions and collections of such contributions.
evidence: The study demonstrated that calibration curves can be used for attribution in open world cases and in cases with lower overall accuracy.

article_title: **Poster: Understanding Newcomers Success in Open Source Community**
actionable: Contribute to multiple projects to increase popularity in OSS.
impact: Helps a newcomer gain more socio-technical skills and followers.
evidence: Analysis of 473 newcomers' activities on GitHub, showing that popular newcomers joined younger projects and contributed to multiple projects.

article_title: **Poster: Understanding Newcomers Success in Open Source Community**
actionable: Prioritize joining younger projects with fewer core committers during initial onboarding.
impact: Improve chances of gaining popularity and success as a newcomer.
evidence: Random Forest feature importance analysis identified project age and core committer count as key selection factors, with empirical results showing popular newcomers specifically targeted younger projects.

article_title: **Poster: Understanding Newcomers Success in Open Source Community**
actionable: Actively participate in code review processes and follow other community members on GitHub.
impact: Increase popularity and reach high status within the open source community.
evidence: Data indicated that successful newcomers gained status by engaging in coordination activities, following members, and participating in reviews rather than relying solely on commit counts.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Community Collaboration and Engagement

actionable: Adopt an approach that combines natural language information and execution information for detecting duplicate bug reports.
impact: Improves recall rates by 18-26 percentage points compared to using only natural language information.
evidence: Experimental results show a recall range of 67%-93% in the Firefox bug repository, compared to 43%-72% using natural language alone.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Apply a classification-based heuristic to rank retrieved bug reports by distinguishing whether natural language or execution information is the dominant factor for each pair.
impact: Outperforms basic heuristics and improves suggested list quality, allowing triagers to achieve high recall by examining fewer reports.
evidence: Calibration on Eclipse demonstrated that the classification-based heuristic consistently outperformed basic and reverse classification heuristics across all tested suggested-list sizes.

actionable: Ignore methods with very small inverse document frequency (idf) in execution traces to optimize storage and calculation costs.
impact: Decreases the computational burden of storing execution information and calculating execution similarity (E-S).
evidence: Section 6.1 explains that frequently appearing methods have small idf values, and removing them reduces index terms and processing time.

actionable: Use only the bug report summary rather than the full description when evaluating larger suggested-list sizes.
impact: Improves detection performance by reducing noise from detailed descriptions that can obscure relevant clues in longer lists.
evidence: Experiments on Eclipse and Firefox showed that using only the summary outperformed using both summary and description when suggested-list sizes became larger.

actionable: Migrate existing bug repositories to support execution information by marking historical reports with "missing" execution data and requesting it for new non-patch submissions.
impact: Enables gradual adoption of the approach without disrupting current workflows or requiring immediate full reproduction of past bugs.
evidence: Section 6.2 outlines a strategy where missing execution data is handled by calculating average E-S, ensuring ranking relies on natural language similarity during transition.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Adopt program splicing as a methodology to automate code completion tasks.
impact: Significantly boost programmer productivity and reduce development time.
evidence: User study with 18 participants showed that using Splicer could complete programming tasks faster than traditional methods, with an average reduction in completion time across multiple problems.

actionable: Write draft programs containing explicit placeholder holes and accompany them with Javadoc-style comments that include 'COMMENT' sections for search hints and 'REQ' sections for correctness requirements.
impact: Enables the synthesizer to efficiently query large codebases and automatically fill holes with valid, requirement-matching codelets.
evidence: The system successfully completed 15 diverse benchmark problems in under two minutes on average, requiring no more than five tests per draft, by leveraging these natural language and test-based hints.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Code Standards and Maintainability | Documentation Practices

actionable: When standard input-output testing is impractical for complex tasks, specify correctness requirements using API call sequence constraints modeled as finite automata within the 'REQ' section.
impact: Effectively filters invalid candidate programs during synthesis and reduces the burden of specifying low-level implementation details.
evidence: Applied to a face detection task, this approach allowed the synthesizer to verify API invocation order via an internal state-tracking environment, completing the synthesis in 8.1 seconds without manual test case construction.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Documentation Practices

actionable: Adopt interprocedural path-sensitivity in static analysis tools to accurately track program paths across function calls.
impact: Improves precision by avoiding false positives from context-insensitive analyses, especially for error handling chains and long call sequences.
evidence: CALYSTO's interprocedural approach identified real bugs in large open-source applications with a low false positive rate of below 23%.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Implement bit-precise analysis in static checkers to handle machine arithmetic accurately.
impact: Reduces false positives and improves precision, especially for boundary conditions and non-linear operators.
evidence: CALYSTO's bit-precision incurs high computational cost but is justified by frequent bug sources like overflows and the need for precise arithmetic handling.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Maintain definitions of interprocedural control-flow context, variables, and abstract memory locations in the analysis
impact: Increased precision by keeping track of these details, reducing false positives
evidence: Context-sensitive analyses that differentiate the effects of a program's state at different call sites are more precise than context-insensitive ones

actionable: Develop application-specific theorem provers optimized for software verification conditions, like SPEAR.
impact: Improves performance and efficiency in handling complex verification conditions with bit-accurate arithmetic.
evidence: SPEAR won the bitvector arithmetic category in the SMT 2007 competition and provided a 500-fold speedup over manually optimized versions.

article_title: **The Scent of a Smell: An Extensive Comparison between Textual and Structural Smells**
actionable: Consider using textual analysis tools like TACO for detecting code smells, as they can identify problematic instances that may be missed by structural approaches.
impact: Textually detected code smells are perceived as harmful and easier to identify and refactor, leading to a higher likelihood of resolution.
evidence: Study involving 301 releases and 183,514 commits from 20 open source projects, and interviews with 19 industrial developers and 5 software quality experts.

actionable: Offer components under dual or tri-licensing schemes to provide downstream users with multiple license options.
impact: Accommodates different user groups with incompatible needs and supports business models that combine open source and proprietary licensing.
evidence: Documented as a common pattern in the study of 124 OSS packages, with known implementations in Perl, Mozilla Core, MySQL, and QT.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Issue license exceptions as addenda to explicitly permit specific uses that are otherwise incompatible with the base open source license.
impact: Facilitates the integration of modules with otherwise incompatible licenses and avoids the proliferation of multiple license versions.
evidence: Identified through a manual analysis of 124 OSS packages, with documented implementations including the Trolltech GPL Exception, MySQL AB FLOSS License Exception, and OpenSSL GPL Exception.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Issue formal clarifications for ambiguous or contentious license terms to reduce legal uncertainty for downstream users.
impact: Clearly communicates licensor intent and allows licensees to understand interpretations in advance, preventing legal disputes.
evidence: Identified in the analysis of 124 OSS packages, with examples including Linux GPL clarifications by Linus Torvalds, Perl GPL clarification, and Eclipse plugin API clarifications.
CATEGORY: Project Management and Governance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Distribute modifications as patches rather than full derivative works when redistribution is restricted or maintaining a fork is undesirable.
impact: Circumvents the need to distribute a derivative work and permits modification without explicit copyright owner approval, while allowing testing of experimental features.
evidence: Documented as a licensee pattern in the study of 124 OSS packages, with examples including MySQL AB's patch repository and Trolltech QT's original Q Public License approach.
CATEGORY: Project Management and Governance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Document and follow the rationale for allowing license mismatches in your software application
impact: Allows a software application to be legally created with components with different licenses (the license-mismatch problem)
evidence: We examined the licensing for 124 OSS projects and documented the rationale for allowing any license mismatches
CATEGORY: Documentation Practices | Project Management and Governance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Use a license that is compatible with as many open source licenses as possible, such as the MIT or Apache licenses
impact: Increases the potential use of your software in other projects and avoids legal issues related to incompatible licenses
evidence: Table 1 shows the frequency of occurrence of different open source licenses and their compatibility, with the MIT/X11 and Apache licenses being the most compatible
CATEGORY: Project Management and Governance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Structure application architecture to ensure reused components are legally classified as part of a collective work rather than a derivative work.
impact: Allows the final application to maintain its own license without being forced into the restrictive terms of the component's license.
evidence: Listed as a standard licensee pattern in Table 2 based on the dependency graph analysis of 124 OSS packages.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Permit re-licensing of derivative works under a different license.
impact: Resolves license mismatches by allowing alternative licensing.
evidence: Java Classpath exception allows linking without GPL restrictions.
CATEGORY: Project Management and Governance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Use add-on patterns to extend functionality via APIs without license conflicts.
impact: Enables component extension while maintaining license compliance.
evidence: Eclipse clarifies plugin API usage avoids derivative work issues.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Select components with compatible licenses to prevent mismatches.
impact: Reduces legal complexities during component integration.
evidence: Tools like FOSSology help identify compatible components.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Ask licensors for exceptions or clarifications to resolve issues.
impact: Directly addresses specific licensing concerns with licensor input.
evidence: Examples include successful requests in studied projects.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Adopt Gvt for automated detection and reporting of GUI design violations in mobile app development.
impact: Improves efficiency and quality of mobile app development by accurately identifying presentation failures.
evidence: Gvt achieved 98% precision and 96% recall in detecting design violations, outperforming developers who had an average detection rate below 60%.

actionable: Ensure bounding boxes of GUI components do not overlap when creating mock-ups in design tools like Sketch.
impact: Prevents tool resolution failures and ensures accurate component matching during automated verification.
evidence: The paper identifies overlapping bounding boxes as a current restriction, noting that Gvt must use an Intersection over Union metric to resolve them, making non-overlapping designs necessary for reliable analysis. (Sec 7)

actionable: Define areas of dynamic content, such as network-loaded data, to be explicitly ignored during the GUI verification analysis.
impact: Prevents false positive design violation reports caused by changing or non-static app elements.
evidence: The tool allows users to define these areas, and industrial managers highlighted that properly handling dynamic components is essential for increasing the tool's utility and flexibility in practice. (Sec 4.5, Sec 6.3)

actionable: Utilize detailed reports containing annotated screenshots and precise violation descriptions to communicate GUI discrepancies between design and development teams.
impact: Facilitates clear communication, reduces arguments over subtle visual differences, and saves time on discussions.
evidence: Every participant in the utility study found highlighted annotations the most useful element, and industrial managers reported that the tool clarifies subtle violations that previously caused team disputes and saves significant discussion time. (Sec 6.2, Sec 6.3)

article_title: **Software Visualization and Deep Transfer Learning for Effective Software Defect Prediction**
actionable: Use data augmentation when converting code to color images for defect prediction.
impact: Improves the efficacy of the model by increasing the size of the dataset without losing semantic and structural features.
evidence: The method expands the data set six-fold, generating 6 color images from each source code file. Experiments showed that using different permutations had quite comparable performance.

article_title: **Software Visualization and Deep Transfer Learning for Effective Software Defect Prediction**
actionable: Adopt an attention mechanism in deep learning models for defect prediction to focus on key features in different defect images.
impact: Further improves prediction by self-attention feature map input to the next layer, enhancing expressive ability of important features.
evidence: The DTL-DP model employs a self-attention mechanism into the model inspired by good performance in GANs. The attention mechanism makes the feature map generated by layer conv5 be the self-attention feature map input to the next layer, fc6.

article_title: **Software Visualization and Deep Transfer Learning for Effective Software Defect Prediction**
actionable: Set the MK-MMD penalty hyperparameter λ to 1 when training cross-project defect prediction models.
impact: Optimizes the trade-off between classification accuracy and domain adaptation, maximizing the F-measure for predicting defects across different projects.
evidence: Sensitivity analysis in Figure 5(a) shows that the F-measure for CPDP peaks at λ = 1, confirming it as the optimal penalty value for aligning source and target project distributions. (Section 3.3)

article_title: **Software Visualization and Deep Transfer Learning for Effective Software Defect Prediction**
actionable: Fine-tune all five convolutional layers of a pre-trained deep learning model instead of freezing the initial layers during the training phase.
impact: Reduces the distribution gap between source code images and the original pre-training dataset, enabling more effective feature extraction for defect prediction.
evidence: The framework explicitly fine-tunes conv1-conv5 layers using ImageNet 2012 parameters as initialization to minimize differences between code images and actual object images, outperforming standard Deep Adaptation Networks that freeze early layers. (Section 3.2)

actionable: Use VulCurator to detect vulnerability-fixing commits in OSS projects.
impact: Improves the accuracy of vulnerability-fixing commit detection by up to 16.1% compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
evidence: Experimental results show that VulCurator outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines up to 16.1% in terms of F1-score.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Implement automated commit-issue linking mechanisms to recover missing links for commits that lack explicit issue associations.
impact: Ensures comprehensive vulnerability monitoring by accurately classifying unlinked commits and boosting overall detection accuracy.
evidence: The authors note that only a fraction of commits are explicitly linked to issues, and limiting the issue linker's similarity threshold ensures accurate recovery, which directly improves classification performance.
CATEGORY: Project Management and Governance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Leverage pre-trained deep learning models, such as RoBERTa for natural language and CodeBERT for code changes, when developing or selecting vulnerability-fixing commit detectors.
impact: Significantly improves classification accuracy compared to traditional machine learning methods or single-source approaches.
evidence: VulCurator's use of pre-trained models improved the F1-score by 16.1% over HERMES on the SAP dataset and by 8.5% on the TensorFlow dataset.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Use Testler to automatically identify and remove fine-grained redundant test statements in Java/JUnit4 test suites.
impact: Reduces test suite execution time while preserving code coverage, test assertions, and fault detection capability.
evidence: Evaluation on 15 open source projects showed an average 20% reduction in execution time (up to 37%), a 43% decrease in redundant statements, and maintained mutation scores and coverage.

actionable: Customize the granularity of the test reorganization analysis to balance readability with redundancy reduction when merging test cases.
impact: Optimizes the trade-off between maintaining readable test suites and maximizing redundancy elimination.
evidence: The authors note that merging tests might affect readability, but practitioners can adjust analysis granularity accordingly; Testler also maintains links between original and minimized versions for traceability.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Apply fine-grained test minimization techniques to UI, mobile, or web testing domains where execution overhead is high.
impact: Substantially decreases test execution time by reducing calls to browser APIs and server-side requests.
evidence: The authors state that web/mobile tests have higher running costs due to GUI/network latency, and minimizing them would yield substantial runtime savings compared to unit tests.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

article_title: **HireBuild: An Automatic Approach to History-Driven Repair of Build Scripts**
actionable: Adopt automated, history-driven repair tools that generate patches for Gradle build scripts based on historical fix patterns and build log similarity.
impact: Reduces the manual effort and time developers spend resolving build failures.
evidence: The proposed approach successfully fixed 11 out of 24 reproducible build failures (45%) with a median repair time of 44 minutes, comparable to the median manual fix time of 42 minutes.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

article_title: **HireBuild: An Automatic Approach to History-Driven Repair of Build Scripts**
actionable: Synchronize build script version dependencies with the actual build environment to prevent compatibility issues.
impact: Avoids build breakage caused by mismatched dependency versions and environment configurations.
evidence: The authors observed that changing dependency versions while retaining an outdated build environment frequently causes failures, particularly in Android projects where SDK and build tool versions are explicitly defined in the script.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

article_title: **Open Source barriers to entry, revisited: A sociotechnical perspective**
actionable: Adopt the GenderMag method to evaluate tools and infrastructure for gender inclusiveness.
impact: Improves inclusivity and reduces barriers, especially for women newcomers.
evidence: Fixing issues identified using GenderMag led to a significant increase in customer satisfaction (Burnett et al., 2017).

article_title: **Open Source barriers to entry, revisited: A sociotechnical perspective**
actionable: Adopt a socio-technical perspective when addressing tool and infrastructure issues in OSS projects, rather than focusing solely on technical bugs or UI fixes.
impact: Lead to more inclusive tools and environments that better support newcomers and diverse contributors by addressing community processes and cultural hurdles embedded in the software.
evidence: The study found that 92% of identified issues matched established newcomer barrier types, with only 42% related to technical hurdles or documentation, while 58% stemmed from community-oriented and cultural barriers manifested through the tools.
CATEGORY: Community Collaboration and Engagement | Project Management and Governance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

article_title: **Open Source barriers to entry, revisited: A sociotechnical perspective**
actionable: Explicitly define technical terminology, contribution workflows, and interface actions in project documentation to prevent confusion and support comprehensive information processing styles.
impact: Reduce cognitive load and risk aversion for newcomers, preserving their computer self-efficacy and encouraging sustained contribution.
evidence: Analysis identified undefined terminology and unexplained processes as key barriers; 88% of identified barriers were linked to computer self-efficacy, and 71%-72% to motivations, risk aversion, and learning styles, indicating that unclear tools actively erode newcomer confidence.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Documentation Practices

actionable: Use the NNLRank recommender system for developer onboarding in GitHub projects.
impact: Improves the quality of recommended projects for developer onboarding, outperforming baselines by 29.81% (mean MRR)
evidence: NNLRank achieves the best performance (mean MRR = 0.466), outperforming the best baseline SVMRank by 29.81%

actionable: Consider using a list-wise ranking loss function for optimizing neural network models in similar contexts.
impact: Improves the performance of neural network models by better handling dependencies between ranked items
evidence: NNLRank, which uses a list-wise ranking loss function, outperforms other baselines with a mean MRR of 0.466

actionable: Hide or remove configuration parameters that are seldom set by any user, and implement user-feedback loops to track configuration settings.
impact: Significantly reduces the configuration space complexity without impacting existing users, making configuration less error-prone.
evidence: Up to 54.1% of parameters are rarely set by any user; applying this guideline removed 51.9% of parameters in Storage-A with an impact on fewer than 1% of users.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Community Collaboration and Engagement

actionable: Promote frequently used configuration parameters to 'first-class' status and include them prominently in tutorials and guidebooks.
impact: Helps users focus on essential settings and achieve an easier, quicker start without skimming through thick manuals.
evidence: Only 1.8% to 7.8% of parameters are configured by more than 90% of users, yet these provide necessary runtime information that is hard to default.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Documentation Practices

actionable: Convert numeric parameters into simpler types like Boolean or enumerative with representative values.
impact: Simplifies settings without losing much flexibility.
evidence: Up to 47.4% of numeric parameters had no more than five distinct settings among users.

actionable: Limit enumerative parameters to a maximum of five options to prevent over-designed flexibility and user confusion.
impact: Reduces configuration complexity by eliminating ambiguous or excessive options that users rarely utilize.
evidence: For enumerative parameters with many options, typically only two to three options are actually used by the majority of users.

actionable: Only expose configuration parameters that have explicit semantics and visible external system impact, hiding those specific to internal implementation.
impact: Increases user confidence in modifying settings and reduces misconfigurations caused by misunderstanding internal mechanics or lacking source code access.
evidence: Parameters with explicit external impact are set by significantly more users, while internal implementation parameters are seldom set because users lack the time or capability to read the code.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Enhance NLP-based configuration navigation tools by boosting match scores with real-world user configuration statistics.
impact: Significantly improves the accuracy of returning target configuration parameters for user queries compared to using parameter names alone.
evidence: Boosting results with configuration statistics improved NLP-based navigation performance, successfully resolving over 60% of historical navigation issues.

actionable: Integrate user-generated content from Q&A forums and mailing lists into configuration navigation support systems.
impact: Provides more targeted and useful information for resolving specific configuration problems compared to dense official manuals.
evidence: User-generated pages contribute over 50% of useful Web pages returned by search engines for configuration navigation, as they record specific user experiences and solutions.
CATEGORY: Community Collaboration and Engagement | Documentation Practices

article_title: **On the Diffuseness and the Impact on Maintainability of Code Smells: A Large Scale Empirical Investigation**
actionable: Assess each code smell case before deciding to refactor.
impact: Improving maintainability by avoiding unnecessary refactoring efforts.
evidence: Classes affected by code smells are more change- and fault-prone, but their removal may not always benefit maintainability.

article_title: **On the Diffuseness and the Impact on Maintainability of Code Smells: A Large Scale Empirical Investigation**
actionable: Consider the magnitude of code smells when assessing their impact on maintainability.
impact: A better understanding of which types of smells are most harmful and where efforts should be focused.
evidence: Previous work did not take into account the magnitude of observed phenomena. Our study showed that some smells can be more harmful than others, depending on their frequency in software projects.

actionable: Discriminate structural dependencies further, considering inheritance as an independent concept in modularization tools.
impact: This improves the impact of inheritance dependencies on modularity.
evidence: Structural dependencies (SD) show high coupling-modularity congruence, with inheritance (SD.Inh) being particularly effective.

actionable: Include Type I clone information in modularization tools to enhance coupling data.
impact: Type I clones provide good average congruence and can improve tool effectiveness.
evidence: Type I clones (CC.I) show high congruence values, indicating their relevance to modularity.

actionable: Consider discerning external and internal fan-out in fan-out information (FO), as they have clearly different congruence to modularity.
impact: Better understanding of the system's modular structure and improved clustering results.
evidence: Study by Andritsos and Tzerpos (2005) found that information-theoretic software clustering can be improved with additional meta-information, including fan-out similarity.

actionable: Combine multiple independent coupling concepts rather than relying on a single dimension when developing or using modularity tools for tasks like software clustering or aspect mining.
impact: Improves the effectiveness of automated modularization approaches and modularity-related applications by leveraging diverse coupling information to better manage system complexity.
evidence: The correlation matrix showed that different coupling concepts are largely statistically independent, and prior studies combining structural dependencies with evolutionary couplings successfully improved clustering results.

actionable: Respond to issues promptly and make a good faith effort to incorporate pull requests, fix issues, and add features as needs arise.
impact: Reduce the need for hard forks by addressing community concerns before they escalate into project splits.
evidence: Interviewee P16 explicitly adopted this practice to reduce the need for hard forks; unresponsive maintainers and rejected PRs were identified as common triggers for hard forks (Sec 4.2).

actionable: Explicitly credit contributors in release notes to retain them in the community.
impact: Keep contributors engaged and prevent disengagement or forking due to lack of recognition.
evidence: Interviewee P14 suggested this practice to keep contributors stay in the community (Sec 4.2).

actionable: Develop improved tooling for managing changes across diverged forks.
impact: Enhances collaboration and integration between hard forks and upstream projects.
evidence: Current tools are inadequate, as noted in the paper's discussion of coordination challenges.
CATEGORY: Community Collaboration and Engagement | Project Management and Governance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Create contributing guides and issue templates to coordinate with contributors more efficiently.
impact: Streamline contributor onboarding and reduce friction that can lead to project fragmentation.
evidence: Interviewee P2 implemented these artifacts specifically to coordinate with contributors more efficiently (Sec 4.2).

actionable: Implement early warning systems, such as external bots, to alert upstream maintainers of emerging hard forks.
impact: Enable maintainers to encourage collaboration over competition and fragmentation if desired.
evidence: Proposed in Sec 4.4 as a practical tooling solution to manage the tension between social and hard forks and prevent community fragmentation.

actionable: Establish personalized stress or overtime detection for at least two thirds of developers that follow regular rhythm.
impact: Improved health and well-being for developers who follow office hours.
evidence: Two clusters (green and black lines) follow typical office hours where commits are concentrated on day time hours during the work week, with clear dips during lunch hour. These two clusters contain 66% of all developers.

actionable: Monitor deviations from historical baseline activity rather than applying fixed thresholds to identify potential project overload or stress.
impact: Accurately flags genuine increases in abnormal work hours (e.g., overtime) while ignoring normal project-specific baselines, preventing unnecessary interventions and supporting sustainable maintenance practices.
evidence: The authors state that 'committing 70% of work during typical working hours might be a stress signal for a project that has previously had a share of 90%, but not for another project that constantly commits 70% work during typical working hours.'

actionable: Avoid using commit timestamps as a proxy for working hours when monitoring project managers or non-technical contributors.
impact: Prevents misleading stress or workload assessments for roles that involve less direct code contribution, ensuring accurate workload tracking across all project roles.
evidence: The authors observed that 'management positions require less technical work and more communication and coordination,' leading to the conclusion that 'for managers, using commits as working hour indicators could be misleading.'

article_title: **TODO or To Bug:  Exploring How Task Annotations Play a Role in the Work Practices of Software Developers**
actionable: Design tools that automatically link in-code task annotations to external issue tracking software and allow verification or removal upon parent task completion.
impact: Supports subtask management workflows and ensures tasks are properly closed or migrated out of the codebase.
evidence: The study identified a gap between formal issue tracking systems and informal code annotations, with developers using TODOs for subtasks but lacking seamless migration mechanisms.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Project Management and Governance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

article_title: **TODO or To Bug:  Exploring How Task Annotations Play a Role in the Work Practices of Software Developers**
actionable: Implement automatic mechanisms for developers to enter and save metadata directly into in-code task annotations.
impact: Facilitates identification and navigation of comments for both creators and other users.
evidence: Survey data showed 51% of developers add initials, 44% add bug IDs, and 30% add URLs to TODOs; the authors explicitly state an automatic way for entering this information would be useful.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Documentation Practices | Project Management and Governance

article_title: **TODO or To Bug:  Exploring How Task Annotations Play a Role in the Work Practices of Software Developers**
actionable: Enhance task filtering capabilities in IDEs to allow easier management and visibility control of annotations.
impact: Makes the Task View more useful by enabling developers to focus on relevant tasks.
evidence: Interviewee noted difficulty changing filters, highlighting the need for better customization options.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Project Management and Governance

article_title: **TODO or To Bug:  Exploring How Task Annotations Play a Role in the Work Practices of Software Developers**
actionable: Provide development tools with wizards that assist developers in handling expired task annotations by offering options to remove, migrate, re-schedule, or clear expiration dates.
impact: Helps cleanse old TODOs from the codebase, preventing clutter and improving code comprehension and maintenance.
evidence: Interviews revealed out-of-date annotations clutter code and negatively affect comprehension; archival analysis showed less than 15% of studied annotations had a lifespan longer than one month.

article_title: **TODO or To Bug:  Exploring How Task Annotations Play a Role in the Work Practices of Software Developers**
actionable: Schedule periodic, project-wide clean-up processes for task annotations throughout the software release cycle.
impact: Reduces accumulation of outdated annotations that obscure meaningful information and hinder long-term maintenance.
evidence: The study found many TODOs remain indefinitely without review, with some developers leaving projects while annotated tasks remain unintelligible to others.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Use RMiner for refactoring detection in commit history
impact: Improves precision and recall of refactoring detection, reduces noise, and enables novel applications such as online refactoring detection and improved code review tools
evidence: RMiner achieves 98% precision and 87% recall, takes on median 58 ms to analyze a commit, and outperforms previous state-of-the-art tools in execution time and accuracy

actionable: Integrate refactoring detection tools into bug-introducing change analysis techniques to filter out non-behavior-altering modifications.
impact: Improve the accuracy of bug-introducing change identification by avoiding false positives caused by refactorings.
evidence: The article states that utilizing refactoring detection can 'avoid flagging changes that do not alter the program behavior (i.e., refactorings) as bug-introducing,' directly addressing noise in tools like SZZ.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Incorporate refactoring detection capabilities into code review and diff visualization tools to abstract or highlight refactoring-related changes.
impact: Help developers better understand code evolution and reduce distraction during code reviews caused by text diffs masking actual developer intent.
evidence: The authors note that 'refactorings distract developers during code reviews' and that integrating detection can 'raise the level of abstraction for code changes originating from refactorings.'
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Leverage refactoring detection to automatically recover or update traceability links between requirements and source code after structural changes are applied.
impact: Maintain accurate requirement-to-code traceability despite frequent structural refactorings that typically break these links.
evidence: The article explicitly suggests that tools tracing requirements to code 'could use RMiner to recover traceability links that are broken due to applied refactorings.'
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Documentation Practices

actionable: Adopt BugZoo for managing and interacting with software bugs in Open Source Software projects.
impact: Improves reproducibility, extensibility, and usability by using Docker containers to isolate dependencies and avoid conflicts.
evidence: BugZoo uses Docker containers to package, deliver, and interact with bugs and tools, ensuring reliable and immutable behavior. This approach avoids DLL hell and reduces performance penalties compared to VMs.
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | Community Collaboration and Engagement | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Integrate existing datasets and tools into decentralized platforms by adding machine-readable YAML manifest files to their hosting Git repositories.
impact: Enables non-invasive platform connectivity, allows independent extension of datasets, and prevents centralization bottlenecks while preserving developer ownership.
evidence: The text notes that support requires "only a small number of supplementary files" and that this decentralized approach "allows users to independently add their tools and datasets" without compromising control or scalability.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Documentation Practices | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Utilize containerized isolated execution environments when reproducing or interacting with historical software bugs.
impact: Guarantees reproducible, immutable program behavior across varying host configurations and eliminates environment-dependent test flakiness.
evidence: The article emphasizes that snapshot behavior depends on exact compile- and run-time configurations, and containers provide an "isolated execution environment" that ensures reliability compared to natural-language build instructions which "does not ensure this reproducibility."
CATEGORY: Automated Testing and Quality Assurance | CI/CD and DevOps Automation

actionable: Adopt Enlighten as an interactive feedback-driven fault localization technique to improve debugging processes.
impact: Enlighten significantly improves fault localization efficiency, reducing the number of interactions needed and the time developers spend on debugging tasks.
evidence: In evaluations with simulated users, over 96% of faults were localized within less than 10 interactions. In user studies, participants using Enlighten performed 39-59% better in terms of both fault localization success and time efficiency compared to traditional methods.

actionable: Incorporate developer feedback as weighted virtual tests to dynamically update statistical fault localization scores during the debugging session.
impact: Rapidly refines suspiciousness rankings and improves localization accuracy by heavily weighting focused human insights over initial test data.
evidence: Assigning a weight of 1 to feedback-encoded virtual tests versus 0.1 for initial tests reduced the average number of required queries by 34% compared to configurations ignoring weights.

actionable: When multiple failing tests exist, prioritize generating debugging queries for the test that triggers the fewest method calls.
impact: Simplifies trace analysis and reduces the cognitive load required to understand execution paths during debugging.
evidence: The authors state that 'shorter traces should be easier to debug,' and their evaluation shows Enlighten localized over 96% of faults with fewer than 10 interactions.

actionable: Re-evaluate the process for socializing new developers and awarding committer status in Open Source Software (OSS) projects.
impact: Improves understanding of participation dynamics in modern OSS ecosystems, potentially enhancing project sustainability and contribution quality.
evidence: The study found that only 8.95% of members followed the onion model within individual projects, suggesting a need to update traditional socialization processes.
CATEGORY: New Contributor Onboarding and Involvement | Community Collaboration and Engagement | Project Management and Governance

actionable: Developers should consider using logical commits to create a network of source code, and then use eigenvector centrality as a metric for scoring the centrality of each file in the network at each time period.
impact: Allows for a more complete network-based view of the project history and source code, and identifies the files that are considered to be most central to the project.
evidence: Eigenvector centrality is robust, avoids issues with network structure, and works for projects that use multiple programming languages. It tends to be high for nodes connected to many other nodes with high eigenvector centrality, while it tends to be low for nodes with few connections to other low scoring nodes.

actionable: Project administrators should attribute the centrality score of the file to the developer who committed it, and generate an overall source code centrality score for each developer by summing the centralities for each of the commits.
impact: Allows for understanding how a developer progresses within the community, and identifying important contributors to the project.
evidence: Developers typically make numerous commits during each community release cycle, and contributions often touch multiple files. Therefore, attributing the centrality score of the file to the developer who committed it is necessary for understanding how a developer progresses within the community.

actionable: Prioritize the development of fault localization techniques that accurately pinpoint exact fix locations rather than relying on noisy spectrum-based rankings.
impact: Reduce the number of generated patch candidates by an order of magnitude and increase the likelihood of generating correct patches.
evidence: Providing ground-truth fix locations to repair tools reduced their median NPC scores substantially (e.g., SimFix dropped from ~200 to ~20) and improved correctness ratios for most tools.

actionable: Implement a halting threshold based on the number of in-plausible patches generated during repair attempts.
impact: Increase the correctness ratio of generated plausible patches by stopping the search before excessive resources are wasted on invalid candidates.
evidence: Setting an upper-bound threshold on in-plausible patches increased the correctness ratio for 14 out of 16 tested APR tools (e.g., +11.9% for Cardumen, +11.4% for FixMiner).

actionable: Evaluate the efficiency of automated program repair systems using the number of generated patch candidates instead of execution time or CPU cost.
impact: Enable reproducible, machine-agnostic comparisons of repair tool performance and avoid biases introduced by varying hardware configurations.
evidence: The authors demonstrated that execution times for compiling and testing vary drastically across different machines, showing no linear correlation with benchmark properties, making time an unreliable efficiency metric.

actionable: Mine fix templates from clean datasets or specialize them for specific bug types when developing template-based repair systems.
impact: Substantially improve repair efficiency by reducing the generation of irrelevant patch candidates.
evidence: The study found that specialized templates (e.g., in AVATAR and FixMiner) lead to lower NPC scores compared to tools using broad, unspecialized template sets like TBar.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Adopt constraint-solving or synthesis strategies over broad heuristic or random search when designing new repair tools.
impact: Drastically reduce the number of generated patch candidates and minimize resource waste during test-based validation.
evidence: Constraint-based tools like ACS exhibited the lowest NPC scores among the 16 evaluated systems, while search-based tools required significantly more attempts to find valid patches.

actionable: Augment standard security keywords with project-specific domain vocabulary when analyzing software development artifacts to identify security issues.
impact: Provides a more accurate picture of a project's security landscape and improves classification performance metrics compared to relying solely on standard or literature-based keyword sets.
evidence: Project-specific vocabulary models achieved the highest recall, precision, and F-Score on their respective oracle datasets (e.g., Derby.model reached 0.917 recall and 0.960 precision), significantly outperforming standard literature vocabularies like Ray.vocab and Pletea.vocab.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Develop classifiers using project-specific security vocabulary to identify security-related messages in software development projects.
impact: Improved accuracy in identifying security issues, as project-specific models outperform standard security terms across datasets.
evidence: Results presented in Tables 2 and 3 show higher recall for project-specific vocabulary models compared to standard security keywords.
CATEGORY: Security Best Practices and Legal Compliance

actionable: Extract timed automata models from Java programs to document and verify their time behavior.
impact: Enables the discovery of bugs in real-time applications and verification of proposed fixes.
evidence: Models were used to find 5 bugs across Apache projects and verify patches.

actionable: Exploit extracted timed automata models to automatically generate regression test suites for time-sensitive code.
impact: Helps developers find out when a bug has been introduced into the software.
evidence: The author states that having a model of the program's time behavior allows it to be exploited to produce a suite of regression tests to detect introduced bugs (Section 2.2).

actionable: Define a time semantics for the Java programming language
impact: Improved precision in detecting time-related errors
evidence: Based on a study of Java's timestamp representation with integer values, which can lead to runtime exceptions

actionable: Analyze source code and create a slice of the original program containing only statements that use or alter identified time variables
impact: Automatic detection of time-related errors in the source code
evidence: Planned research to develop an approach for automatic detection of time errors using SMT solvers as oracles

actionable: Start with predicting comment locations in pull requests as a simpler task before attempting full automation.
impact: Improves understanding of where comments are needed, laying groundwork for further automation.
evidence: The article focuses on predicting comment locations as an initial step, showing it's challenging yet foundational.

actionable: Conduct human subject studies to understand why maintainers comment inconsistently on code changes.
impact: Identifies whether uncertainty is contextual or inherent, guiding better automation strategies.
evidence: Model struggles with high ambiguity, suggesting need for deeper understanding of reviewer behavior.

actionable: Adopt realistic, minimally filtered data distributions when training code review automation models for OSS projects instead of using artificially balanced or synthetic datasets.
impact: Prevents a major loss in practical efficacy caused by distribution mismatch between training data and real-world code reviews.
evidence: The authors explicitly warn that relying on artificial balancing 'risks a major loss in efficacy in practice' and validate their approach using 178,127 PRs across 245 projects with minimal filtering.
CATEGORY: Code Standards and Maintainability | Automated Testing and Quality Assurance

actionable: Consider using a random baseline for review prioritization, as it outperforms some models in certain scenarios.
impact: Provides a simple and effective benchmark for review prioritization tasks.
evidence: Both historical and cross-project models clearly outperform a random baseline in Figure 3.

actionable: Use Perceval to gather software project data from various sources
impact: Simplifies and unifies data collection, enabling further analysis and insights
evidence: Demonstrated in the paper through multiple examples and use cases

impact: Enables powerful data exploration and visualization through tools like Kibana.
evidence: The JSON documents can be stored in an ElasticSearch database and visualized with Kibana dashboards.

actionable: Adopt Perceval to simplify data collection from multiple open source development tools.
impact: Enables efficient and consistent gathering of project data, improving software analytics capabilities.
evidence: Perceval covers over 20 well-known tools and platforms related to contributing to open source development.

actionable: Use Perceval as a Python library for embedding its functionality into custom scripts.
impact: Facilitates integration with existing workflows and tools, enhancing flexibility.
evidence: Listing 4 demonstrates how to use Perceval in a Python script.

actionable: Utilize Perceval's incremental support for efficient data gathering over time.
impact: Reduces redundant work and improves efficiency by fetching only new or updated data.
evidence: The _from-date_ argument allows fetching commits from a specific date, showing incremental support.

actionable: Consider using the 'relates' link type in Jira issue tracking systems to largely capture textual similarity of connected issues.

evidence: An average achieved recall@10 of 39% for C2 cases, where both related issues are either features or improvements, indicates high textual similarity.

actionable: Use net-size measurements that exclude comments, whitespace, and dead code instead of gross Lines of Code when estimating development effort.
